chapters.file: ch22 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Levi Bryant uses the D&D universe to expound a 'flat ontology' of active substances: every entity, from enchanted swords to white dragons, has a virtual proper being (powers or 'affects') that actualizes variable 'local manifestations' depending on circumstances like lighting or armor. Adopting Andy Clark and David Chalmers's extended mind hypothesis, he argues a blind man with a cane, a smartphone owner, or Elric wielding Stormbringer is a literally different mind or entity, and that alliances (Raistlin's Staff of Magius, a warrior's plate armor) generate genuinely new powers rather than mere tool-use. Against Democritus's atomism, he holds aggregates can be individuals, and the game's dice embody his claim that chance produces necessity: throws generate 'regimes of attraction' no DM or player controls. D&D thus mirrors our own world of hidden powers, aleatory encounters and collectives of humans and nonhumans.

chapters.file: ch23 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Monica Evans asks what relationship holds between a player and a character, opening with Plutarch's Ship of Theseus to probe whether a character rebuilt under a new edition, recreated in Neverwinter Nights, or played in succession by two people is still the 'same' character. She applies James Paul Gee's three identities (virtual, real-world, projective) to Wil Wheaton playing Aeofel, whose in-character chase of Leer into an acid pit shows projective identity trumping good gameplay. Worch's 'identity bubble', Bartle's four player types, and the management of player versus character knowledge (the veteran whose wizard meets a bulette, the INT 7 barbarian Dak) frame D&D as a shared fiction in which players explore who they are or might be.

chapters.file: ch24 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy.md
ch25 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Ehrett and Worth ask whether D&D is really a game and why we invest so much in it. Against the Socratic model (the Euthyphro dialogue's search for a common thread defining piety, here applied to 'game'), they deploy Wittgenstein's family-resemblance account from the Philosophical Investigations, concluding D&D lacks clear winning and losing but is rule-governed, with the twist that rule-breaking is legitimate exactly when it serves the game's primary purpose of group storytelling. They then take up the paradox of fiction: since players know the world is not real, Radford's puzzle arises, and Kendall Walton's make-believe theory of props and fictional truths supplies their answer, making D&D an especially gripping fiction because players are participants rather than observers.

chapters.file: ch26 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Wolfendale and Franklin argue D&D is a genuine art form with its own aesthetic. Tracing the medium's birth from Gygax's Chainmail to Arneson's invention of the persistent campaign setting, they use Kant's account of aesthetic experience from the Critique of Judgment, in which disinterested pleasure arises from the 'free play' of the cognitive faculties, and claim that in role-playing that free play just is the collaborative generation of a fictional world. The result is 'depth': consequences no one planned, like a sorcerer Polymorphing a spider demon into a purple platypus or a fumbled Bluff check turning a session into a prison break. This pleasurable because it exercises, under realistic friction and constraint from rules and dice, the mind's world-building power.

chapters.file: ch27 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Chris Bateman’s “The Rules of Imagination” argues RPG rules function primarily as prescriptions for what to imagine rather than as regulations of conduct: Saving Throws, classes, character-sheet attributes, modules, maps, and miniatures are all “props” in Kendall Walton’s make-believe theory of representation, with the Dungeon Master’s authorizing word deciding what becomes fictional at the table. It treats dice as props whose appeal ranges from the Platonic solids’ exoticism to gambling’s “favor of destiny” — D&D’s revolution was tying the die roll to a personally inhabited narrative, complete with critical hits and fumbles. It defends character classes against skill-based systems as accessibility aids for less imaginative players, and closes by claiming tabletop RPGs as art: on prop theory, all artworks are games of make-believe, and RPGs are the purest form, “not just experienced, but lived.” (Slugs empty — Walton and prop theory are taxonomy gaps, logged as holes.)

chapters.file: ch28 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Adam Brackin stages the old ludology-versus-narratology fight among game theorists (Juul, Laurel, Costikyan, Rules of Play) and argues D&D refutes both camps: Fourth Edition's rules history, the 'Roll-Playing for Roleplaying' April Fool's joke, and player-versus-character knowledge show that neither rules nor story alone explains the game. Comparing computer RPGs like D&D Online, which are closed systems 'on a rail', with the tabletop's open border region of 'quest' and flow, he invokes the Turing test: no computer game can simulate human interaction believably because AI lacks the human DM's creativity. The real action is the no-man's-land where gameplay and role-play fuse, and gamers were right to shrug at the theorists and roll dice.

chapters.file: ch29 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Timothy Christopher opens with the Zen archer who 'lets the arrow fall' rather than releasing it: once the arrow is in the air it goes where it will, which he offers as a model of Dungeon Mastering, since a DM plans a campaign but cannot control where players take it once play begins. He maps DM mindsets onto two axes (control over the world, control over the characters) yielding four archetypes: the balanced guide, the minimal host, the rule-enforcing arbiter, and the railroad-imposing puppet master, each with its own measure of success. Like a Zen archer who could subtly bend wind and gravity, a crafty DM invisibly influences the arrow in flight, and groups should agree on the preferred style up front to avoid friction.

chapters.file: ch30 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Jason Rose’s “The Gunpowder Crisis” opens with a campaign story where a player’s dwarf alchemist authentically invents gunpowder, forcing the unprepared DM into a fun-destroying “DM is always right” ruling, and uses it to dissect metagaming — the gap between what the player knows and wants and what the character knows and wants. Working through the ludology-versus-narratology debate, it argues metagaming is a tool rather than a vice: DMs may fudge rolls behind the screen, low ability scores can be played as flaws, hero-point systems (Mutants and Masterminds) build narrative editing into the ludology, and dice give an impartial, “neutral ground” source of narrative tension. Its key move is the choice–chance inversion between in-game and metagame perspectives — characters are accountable for dice they never rolled while unaccountable for backgrounds their players chose — resolving the crisis through in-game consequences instead of fiat. (Slugs empty — metagaming and the ludology–narratology debate are taxonomy gaps, logged as holes.)

chapters.file: ch31 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: David Aldridge reads the D&D manuals' ban on 'metagame thinking' through Gadamer's hermeneutics of the 'event of understanding' from Truth and Method. He tests three models of knowing one's character: Collingwood's re-enactment thesis (total immersion, shown impossible by Fourth Edition's bird's-eye battle maps and the intrusion of rules talk), Collingwood's own 're-enactment plus' amendment joined to Husserlian bracketing (holding out-of-character knowledge apart, knowing the author better than he knew himself), and Gadamer's fusion of horizons, grounded in Heidegger's pre-understanding and illustrated by Plato's paradox of learning, in which no clean having-versus-acting distinction on OOC knowledge survives. Because understanding is always being 'brought up short' by what the character sheet cannot capture, playing a character transformationally teaches us about ourselves.

holes.name: Flat Ontology (object-oriented ontology)
holes.what: The view (Levi Bryant's onticology, kindred to object-oriented ontology and Deleuzo-Latourian assemblage theory) that all entities are active substances with virtual powers ('affects') whose qualities are variable local manifestations under local conditions, with no human privilege in the universe.
holes.why: Chapter 22 is an explicit exposition of this framework, using D&D substances, alliances, regimes of attraction and dice-driven chance to argue for it.

holes.name: Levi Bryant
holes.what: Speculative realist philosopher and author of The Democracy of Objects, whose 'onticology' treats objects as powers that actualize differently in local manifestations and enter into transformative alliances.
holes.why: Chapter 22 is Bryant's own chapter expounding his ontology through D&D, and his technical vocabulary (virtual proper being, local manifestation, regime of attraction) has no taxonomy home.

holes.name: Family Resemblance
holes.what: Wittgenstein's account (Philosophical Investigations) that the members of a concept like 'game' are united by overlapping, criss-crossing similarities rather than a single common essence.
holes.why: Chapter 25's central argument that D&D counts as a game, despite lacking winning and losing, is built directly on applying family resemblance to the concept of a game.

holes.name: The Paradox of Fiction
holes.what: The puzzle (Colin Radford) that we have genuine emotional responses to characters we know do not exist, with Kendall Walton's make-believe theory of quasi-emotions and fictional truths as a leading solution.
holes.why: Chapter 25 devotes its second half to this paradox and Walton's answer to explain why players are emotionally gripped by D&D campaigns they know are not real.

holes.name: Kendall Walton
holes.what: Philosopher of art whose make-believe theory of representation (Mimesis as Make-Believe) treats artworks as props that prescribe imaginings within fictional worlds.
holes.why: Chapter 27 is built entirely on Walton's prop theory, using it to explain D&D rules, dice, classes, character sheets and the claim that all games are art.

holes.name: Make-Believe Theory of Representation (props)
holes.what: Kendall Walton's theory that representations are props prescribing specific imaginings, generating truths 'fictional' within a game of make-believe.
holes.why: Chapter 27 applies prop theory to every component of D&D (rules, dice, classes, attributes, modules, maps, miniatures) as its organizing framework.

holes.name: Ludology vs Narratology
holes.what: The game-studies debate over whether games should be understood primarily as rule-based formal systems (ludology) or as extensions of narrative (narratology).
holes.why: Chapter 28 frames the whole role-play versus gameplay question through this divide and locates D&D's essence in the border region between the two camps.

holes.name: Metagaming (player vs character knowledge)
holes.what: The use of out-of-character knowledge or game-level reasoning by players or DMs, and the craft of distinguishing and managing what players know versus what their characters know.
holes.why: Chapter 30's entire account of the gunpowder crisis, fudged rolls, hero points and the choice-chance inversion rests on the concept of the metagame.

holes.name: R.G. Collingwood
holes.what: British idealist philosopher of history whose 're-enactment thesis' holds that historical understanding is re-thinking the thoughts of historical agents, later amended so the historian must also know that he is re-enacting.
holes.why: Chapter 31 builds its first two models of player-character understanding directly on Collingwood's re-enactment thesis as presented through Gadamer's Truth and Method.
